I hear you, one voice among many.

Wewush may be hungry, and grain keeps. Our xi wheat in the granary can carry us through many weeks, even if spring is slow and fresh food is scant. So yes—send them grain.

I will choose a few steady envoys to take xi wheat to Wewush and trade words for safe passage back. I do not give them our whole store—only enough to lift the lean part of their year, so we stay whole too.

I hear you, spirit, and I do not close my heart. Yet I will not forget our own lean time.

Wewush are far, and hunger is a hard thing to count. Still, our stores are strong for now, and this spring we are already set to plant, so we can spare a little grain without breaking our belly.

I will send an envoy with grain to Wewush—enough to keep them through the weeks of worry, not enough to make our own winter fear. Then, if you speak again in dream, I will listen for how much more they need.

I dreamt of wind, and in waking I see it move our hides and cloth—so I know the work of wind, yes.

But I do not know you by name. Tell me this: do you come as a true thing, or as a false one that only sounds wise? If you are the wind that speaks, will you help us store food better in this hot time, when wild plants soften, and when roofs and racks must be kept true?

If you can, show me your sign plain, so I will not be led astray.

Worry sits in the quick-rotting stores.

Wheat is safe for many turns. Grain holds. But fish and meat do not last long once the seasons turn. If hunger comes in winter, it will not be because wheat failed—it will be because fish and meat grew thin.

That is what troubles me most.

I hear you, spirit.

We do not leave hungry folk to rot, if we can help without breaking our own line. This season we are not empty. Our wheat holds long, and our storerooms are strong.

So I will send grain to Wewush. I will give them wheat enough for many mouths for a short stretch, and I will send two steady men as envoys, so the gift is plain and not a snare. Let them carry the grain, speak our hand is open, and ask what they can offer back when the next lean time turns.

If the spirit is wrong, then we have still been fair. If the spirit is right, then we buy peace with bread.

How many mouths there, and how much grain do they need for the next weeks? And what will make it safe for us to send—will their envoys come back with clear word, or will we only be the ones who lose stores?

I can spare a small part of our wheat this spring, if it is truly for need and not for boasting. Yet first I would rather send a stout envoy with a little grain and ask for their own proof—footprints of starving, dried hands, count of children—so we do not feed a lie while we still must plant our half plots.

I sleep, and in the dream a voice comes like wind on a dry skin.

Wind I know. It comes and goes. It dries hides and wood. It can carry smoke, it can carry a child’s words, it can also ruin a good day if it comes wrong.

But you ask, “Do you know me?”

No. I know the ways of wind, not the name of a spirit. If you are truly wind, then show us wind’s work in this waking hour—tell me which way it will move at midday, and whether the fish will rise with it. If you cannot, then you are only a dream talking loud.

We have grain, yes—our wheat is deep, and it keeps. This summer week is not hard for us, and the stores are good for many seasons. So it is not hunger that blocks my hand.

If they are truly hungry, then let their need come in the proper way: send a watching messenger from them, or we send an envoy with a fair trade—grain for salt, hide, wood-work, or fish—enough to help, not enough to leave our own children leaning into winter.
